title: Workato
note: Workato's durable design concepts: triggers and jobs, failure and rerun safety, concurrency, promotion and access, PHI controls, governed agent tools and task metering. Plan limits and features are as of Nov 2026; connector specifics, formulas and AI features live in Workato's docs. Refresh quarterly.

concepts.s: Workato is event-driven application integration: a trigger creates a job, actions transform and deliver, reruns replay the stored event, and environments, roles and task metering govern it; heavy batch ELT belongs in the warehouse.

x.b:
• Pattern: trigger (poll, webhook, schedule) to job to actions; each job stores its inputs and outputs.
  • Reliability: retries, idempotent writes, safe reruns, concurrency set deliberately.
  • Governance: DEV to TEST to PROD deployments, project roles, PHI masking and retention.
  • Cost: tasks, roughly one per successful action.
  • Fit: coming from Azure Data Factory, move app integration, APIs and agent tools here; keep heavy transforms in Fabric, Databricks or the warehouse (Workato Data Pipelines can replicate objects, billed per row).
Trap: Porting ADF data flows into recipes: row-by-row loops burn tasks and time.
New patient in the EHR triggers a recipe that creates the billing account and posts to Teams. The nightly 40M-row claims load stays in the data platform.

cards.q: An ADF pipeline copies 40M rows nightly. Should it move to a Workato recipe?
cards.a: No: bulk data movement belongs in Fabric, Databricks or the warehouse; Workato fits event-driven app integration.
Tasks: about one per successfully executed action step.

concepts.s: Every trigger event becomes a job, so choose real-time triggers for latency, polling for simplicity, and filter with trigger conditions so unwanted events never become jobs.

x.b:
• Polling: checks on an interval (as of Nov 2026, default 5 minutes on Professional plans and up, 10 on Base); one poll can create many jobs.
  • Real-time: webhooks push events; many connector triggers add a periodic backup poll; plain HTTP webhooks don't.
  • Scheduled: run at set times, events in batches.
  • Trigger conditions filter before a job exists; batch triggers suit volume.

Trap: Filtering with an IF step after the trigger: the job still runs and clutters history.
Trap: Relying on a plain webhook with no backup poll: a missed delivery is lost.
Trap: A trigger condition on a batch trigger checks only the first record.
Only appointments with status Confirmed should sync: put that in the trigger condition, not a first-step IF.

cards.q: Only 5% of trigger events matter. Where should the filter go?
cards.a: In a trigger condition, so unwanted events never become jobs.

cards.q: Which real-time trigger type lacks a backup poll?

concepts.s: Wrap risky steps in a Monitor block with short retries, end failed paths with Stop job so failures stay visible, and design writes to survive reruns that replay the stored event.

x.b:
• Handle errors: Monitor plus On error; up to 3 retries, 1-10 seconds apart, optionally only when a condition holds (e.g. 429 or 5xx).
  • Branch on structured fields (error type, HTTP status), never the message text.
  • Rerun replays the stored trigger event with the latest recipe version; it does not re-read the source.
  • So writes must be idempotent: upsert on a key, check before create.

Trap: An On error branch that ends without Stop job can leave the job looking successful; failures hide in green lists.
Trap: Seconds-long retries for hour-long outages; fail and reconcile later instead.
Upsert appointment on external ID; On error: notify ops through one recipe function, then Stop job as failed.

cards.q: A rerun created duplicate records in the target. What design fixes it?
cards.a: Idempotent writes: upsert on a stable key instead of create.

cards.q: Failures don't show in the job list even though On error ran. Why?
cards.a: The On error branch ended without Stop job; end it with Stop job so the job is marked failed.

concepts.s: Set recipe concurrency deliberately: 1 preserves event order, more raises throughput but needs order-independent, idempotent steps, and every job runs inside timeouts and plan limits.

x.b:
• Recipe concurrency defaults to 1: jobs run one at a time, roughly in event order (Workato warns order isn't strictly guaranteed).
  • Plan-level concurrency caps the total across recipes.
  • Standard job timeout is 90 minutes; API Platform jobs time out much sooner.
  • Use batch triggers and bulk actions for volume; split long work into recipe functions.
Trap: Raising concurrency on a recipe whose updates must apply in order: later events can land before earlier ones.
Status updates to one patient record must apply in order: keep concurrency 1, or partition by patient and guard with a version check.

cards.q: Throughput is too low but update order matters. What do you weigh?
cards.a: Higher concurrency only if steps are order-independent and idempotent; otherwise keep 1 or add version checks.

cards.q: What do you give up by raising recipe concurrency above 1?
cards.a: Ordering: later events can finish before earlier ones, so steps must be order-independent and idempotent.

concepts.s: Edit only in DEV, deploy projects to TEST and PROD, and grant access through project roles to groups, because deployments overwrite target edits and never delete removed assets.

x.b:
• Environments-enabled workspaces deploy one project at a time from DEV to TEST or PROD; every save creates a version; test cases mock steps and check outputs.
  • Environment roles govern settings; project roles (admin, advanced builder, builder, operator) govern content; collaborator groups assign them.
  • Platform APIs let CI run tests and deploy on merge.

Trap: Deleting a recipe in DEV and expecting the deploy to remove it from PROD. Stop and delete it there.
Trap: Hotfixing in PROD: the next deploy overwrites it.
Builders submit deployment requests; advanced builders or project admins deploy to PROD after test cases pass.

cards.q: A recipe deleted in DEV keeps running in PROD after deployment. Why?
cards.a: Deployments don't delete assets removed from the source; stop and delete it in PROD.

cards.q: A fix was made directly in PROD last week and vanished. Why?
cards.a: The next deploy from DEV overwrote it.

concepts.s: For PHI: sign the BAA, mask sensitive steps, shorten job-data retention, source credentials from a secrets manager, and stream audit logs to your SIEM.

x.b:
• Workato states it can sign BAAs as a business associate; confirm your plan covers it.
  • Mask data per step keeps inputs and outputs out of job history; masked triggers still store the event for reruns until retention expires.
  • Retention (as of Nov 2026): 30 days on Standard and Business, 90 on Enterprise, which can set 1 hour to 90 days. After expiry, reruns are disabled.
  • Secrets from AWS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault and others; audit log streaming to S3, Splunk, Datadog and more.

Trap: PHI in data tables or FileStorage: job retention settings don't cover them.
Trap: PHI in alert messages sent to chat.
Recipe moving lab results: mask the trigger and transform steps, 7-day retention, Key Vault credentials, audit stream to the SIEM.

cards.q: You shortened job retention, but PHI still sits in Workato. Where?
cards.a: Data tables, Workflow apps data or FileStorage, which retention doesn't cover.

cards.q: What do you lose when job data retention expires?
cards.a: Job details and trigger data, and with them the ability to rerun those jobs.

concepts.s: Expose internal systems to AI agents through narrow, governed tools with per-user identity, role-based tool access and audit, rather than broad credentials.

x.b:
• Workato's Enterprise MCP publishes tools from API collections, skills (recipe-based workflows) or proxied third-party MCP servers.
  • OAuth, verified user access (calls run with each user's credentials), tool-level RBAC and audit sit in one place.
  • Tool descriptions decide when an agent calls a tool; mark read-only tools and gate destructive ones.
Trap: Publishing a broad tool like "run arbitrary SQL": agents use it in ways you never tested.
Instead of database credentials for the assistant, publish get_patient_appointments(patient_id, date_range), read-only, callable only by the scheduling group.

cards.q: Why prefer verified user access for agent tools?
cards.a: Each call runs with the end user's own permissions, so the agent can't exceed what that user may see.

cards.q: An agent keeps calling the wrong tool. First fix?
cards.a: Sharpen the tool descriptions, which drive tool selection.

concepts.s: Workato meters chiefly by tasks, one per successful action, so step count per job times job volume is your cost model, and loops are where it explodes.

x.b:
• Skipped, failed and canceled steps don't count; reruns do.
  • Other meters: API calls, data pipeline rows, genie actions, MCP proxy calls, events, seats.
  • Levers: trigger conditions, batch and bulk actions instead of per-row loops, fewer steps per job, lookups in formulas instead of extra actions.
Trap: A loop that updates 10,000 rows one action at a time: 10,000 tasks per job.
Monthly tasks of about 3 actions x 20,000 jobs = 60,000. Adding a trigger condition that skips 70% of events cuts it to about 18,000.

cards.q: A recipe's tasks spiked after a backlog was rerun. Why?
Cheapest way to cut tasks on a high-volume recipe?
cards.a: Filter events with trigger conditions and replace per-row loops with batch or bulk actions.
